## About This Facility
Set adjacent to the Health, Wellness & Athletics (HWA) Complex and encircled by **Earl F. Morris Track** on the north end of Wittenberg's picturesque 100-acre campus, Edwards-Maurer Field serves as the competition home of the Tiger field hockey, football, men's and women's lacrosse, and men's and women's soccer teams. Situated within historic Wittenberg Stadium, Edwards-Maurer Field also hosts outdoor club and intramurals events, in addition to a variety of high school and youth activities throughout the year.
In 2005, the field's knitted nylon artificial surface was replaced with Prestige artificial turf, and a new UBU Sports Speed Series S5-M synthetic turf was laid in 2015. The playing surface is designed to handle year-round, multi-sport use and unpredictable Ohio weather, with the 2015 turf installed by Maumee Bay Turf Center.
The turf upgrade to Edwards-Maurer Field in 2005 coincided with the resurfacing of Earl F. Morris Track with a Recotan surface (work performed by DeFargo Sports Surfaces of Round Rock, Texas), the **opening of the Rosencrans Hall of Honor Fitness Center** and the reconstruction of the staircase leading to the main entrance of the stadium. The men's and women's soccer teams began competing at the field after the installation of the turf, having previously played at Bill Edwards Field, near **Betty Doughman Dillahunt Field**.
texts.2:
## About This Facility
Edwards-Maurer Field stands on a site which has served as the home of Tiger football since 1923, field hockey since 1993, lacrosse since 1968 and soccer since 2005. In 1993, the $2.2 million Bill Edwards Drive Project installed Astroturf, lights (for the first time since 1967) and a new track. On Sept. 8, 1993, a ribbon-cutting ceremony preceded the first intercollegiate game on the new surface, which saw field hockey host Earlham and also served as a celebration of the 100th anniversary of women's athletics at Wittenberg. The dedication of Edwards-Maurer Field occured on Oct. 2, 1993, at halftime of the Homecoming football game vs. Case Western Reserve.
The field has played host to countless Ohio Athletic Conference and North Coast Athletic Conference championships, NCAA Division III postseason games, and regular season thrillers over the years. Even on chilly November nights and wet March afternoons, the Tiger faithful pack the stands.
**Accessibility:** Edwards-Maurer Field and Wittenberg Stadium are fully accessible to individuals with disabilities, and the Athletics staff is happy to make accommodations for interested patrons. The stadium features wheelchair seating at the top of the stands, and both the north and south gates are accessible via wheelchair.
* * *
texts.3:
## About This Facility
###  Bill Edwards
Bill Edwards, Wittenberg class of 1931, was introduced as the university's athletic director and head football coach on April 3, 1955. The Wittenberg University Department of Athletics hasn’t been the same since, rising to a level of prominence in small college athletics that is rivaled by few of its peers.
Edwards, who had high school, college and professional coaching experience before taking a pay cut to return to his alma mater, patrolled the sidelines for three national titles in the 1960s while compiling a 98-20-4 record in 14 years as Wittenberg's head football coach (1955-69). He was later inducted into the National College Football Hall of Fame, one of four Wittenberg athletes or coaches to gain such acclaim, and he was a member of the inaugural class of the university's Athletics Hall of Honor in 1985. He passed away in 1987.
Find more information on his legacy at Wittenberg **in this news release**, commemorating the 50th anniversary of his hiring.
* * *
texts.4:
## About This Facility
###  Dave Maurer
Dave Maurer built a tremendous legacy over 40 years as a coach, administrator and professor. Maurer, a 1987 Wittenberg Athletics Hall of Honor inductee, coached track and field, swimming and diving, and golf at various points during his Wittenberg career, in addition to his well-known exploits on the football sidelines. He also served as the university's director of men's athletics and was a professor of health and physical education. Maurer passed away in 2011 at the age of 79.
After more than a decade as an assistant football coach at Wittenberg, Maurer took the reins in 1969. Through 1983, Maurer posted a career record of 129-23-3, good for an astounding .842 winning percentage, best among active coaches at that time, and he earned national coach of the year honors twice. Along the way, Maurer directed three teams to national championships (and was an assistant coach for two other national titlists) and two teams to NCAA Division III Tournament runner-up finishes. The Tigers went undefeated three times and won seven Ohio Athletic Conference championships in his 15 seasons as head coach, and Maurer was later inducted into the National College Football Hall of Fame.
Find more information on his lasting impact at Wittenberg **in this online feature**, celebrating "Dave Maurer Day" at Wittenberg.
* * *
texts.5:
## About This Facility
### History
The original Wittenberg Stadium _**(pictured left: Zimmerman Field circa 1915)**_ was constructed over 1922 and 1923, and dedicated on Saturday, Oct. 20, of that year, prior to a 14-0 loss to visiting Ohio Wesleyan. Capacity crowds of 5,000 in both the permanent west stands and equally large but temporary east stands, where both student sections were seated, plus standing room only crowds of more than 2,000 set the attendance record of over 12,000. The facility was constructed with concrete stands seating 4,980, at a cost of $100,000. At the time, the _Springfield Daily News_ described the stadium as the second largest college football stadium in Ohio, behind only Ohio Stadium in Columbus, which opened the year before in 1922.
Wittenberg Stadium was built on an abandoned gravel pit directly east of Zimmerman Field, which had served as the school's athletic field since 1902. College President Rees Edgar Tulloss selected the site, and Athletics Director and College Football Hall of Famer Ernie Godfrey and his assistants prepared the playing field. Work on the field included digging out 10,000 cubic yards of earth and replacing it with two feet of conditioned gravel topped by soil and sod at an appropriate slope. Original plans called for the completion of a bowl-type stadium seating 30,000 spectators. Work to secure financing and acquire land began in 1919.
Zimmerman Field had been the first permanent enclosed athletic field at the college before it was succeeded by Wittenberg Stadium. A group of local business leaders led by John L. Zimmerman purchased the land in 1902 and donated it to the school in Zimmerman's name. The first game played at the new field was a scoreless tie with Kenyon on November 27, 1902, the last game of the season.

Last year, a possible new tradition seemed to begin, and it continues in 2026 as the USA Curling Arena National Championship goes to newly christened dedicated curling ice. Dallas/Fort Worth Curling Club is set to host their first national championship in their new facility this week, bringing the event to the most dominant region in the history of arena nationals for the first time.
USA Curling’s Arena National Championships have been held since 2013, and never before has the event been held in the Mid-America region. Despite that, the MACA region has won 4 of 11 championships (three of those by 2026 competitor Alyssa Parks) while the region has been on top of the men’s podium an astounding 8 times. Most of those 8 championships were won by members of Dallas/Fort Worth Curling Club.
Finally, after years of hard work and significant investments of time and money, DFW Curling Club achieved the goal of so many arena clubs: to be ineligible to compete at arena nationals. Their long history of strong showings at nationals is coming to an end for the best reason as they open up their new dedicated facility in Irving, Texas.
The overhead view from Dallas/Fort Worth’s new home in Irving, Texas. Photo: Jim Hicks
It hasn’t been without challenges. If you are on social media, you’ve likely seen that the club was broken into shortly after their grand opening bonspiel last month. Among the stolen items were thousands of dollars’ worth of valuable tools owned by members which were being used in their continued construction.
It was a significant setback for the club in their new facility.
If anything, the arrival of 24 teams from across the country into their new home should be a welcome morale boost. The arriving teams will enter the facility and hopefully take a moment to envision dreams of their own hopeful graduation from arena ice to a new place they can call home.
If you want to help support DFW Curling Club following last months’ break-in so they can recoup some of what they lost and continue making progress on their new home, click the link below:
Donate to Dallas/Fort Worth Curling Club
Let’s dig into this year’s event and meet the teams, learn how to watch, and where to follow along!
DFW Curling offers some streaming through their YouTube channel.

Scores and Standings
Both the men’s and women’s events will feature 12 teams. Because DFW Curling is a 5-sheet club, two teams will be on bye for each draw. The draws will alternate between men’s and women’s draws with the first women’s draw starting at 8pm CST on Wednesday, November 11th.
The top three teams from each pool qualify for the playoffs with the top seed earning a bye into the semifinal.
Teams are listed in order of peer seeding.

Team Asis is back, back again. After qualifying at the Coulee Sweep Last Chance qualifier in La Crosse, Wisconsin a few months ago, Jennifer Asis returns for her fourth consecutive national championship. Teammates Jaclyn Pytlarz and Melissa Wheeler are back for their fifth consecutive event, having played in every championship since it restarted in 2022.
Asis has won a medal of every color over the past three years and is coming off of a bronze medal finish in 2025. The Silicon Valley rink heads back to nationals as an incredibly well-rounded team who posted the best Steal Defense Efficiency rating (not giving up steals when you have hammer) at this championship for the second consecutive year. If they can continue that trend and force their opponents to single points at a high rate, they’ll be in contention for a podium once again.
_Team Asis after their 2024 National Chamiponship in Wausau, WI. Photo: USA Curling_
Jordan Connelly returns for her second consecutive arena national championship after winning the MoPac playdown in back-to-back seasons. Their best-of-three playdown against fellow club members from Team Bonache went the distance, but they emerged victorious. At least year’s championships, Connelly went 3-2 in round robin play before being eliminated in the quarterfinals.

Team Mercer of the Cleveland Skating Club qualified for the Arena National Championship through an uncontested playdown, but don’t let that fool you. This team is in the running every single year at arena nationals. Katy Mercer’s rink has posted fourth-place finishes each of the past two seasons, but they’re no strangers to the podium either. They won gold in 2018 and silver in 2019. They’ll be a tough matchup for everyone and should be considered a playoff contender.
It looked like Kelsey Beyer was on the verge of making the playoffs at last year’s national championship in Las Vegas. The Minnesota rink started the event by beating the eventual national championships, lost a tight game to Jennifer Asis, and entered their final game of pool play with a 2-2 record, just needing a win to qualify. Unfortunately, that last game didn’t go their way.
They boasted the best hammer efficiency rate in the field last year, scoring two points with the hammer in nearly 50% of all of their ends. If they can continue that trend again this season, they’ll have a great chance to advance to the playoffs.

It’s a feat that can be difficult to repeat but also can be very frustrating to play against when successful.

She has a new set of teammates with her this year, and the team has been working hard to improve, traveling to dedicated curling clubs in Wisconsin to get practice ice in preparation for the event.

Historic Edwards Stadium/Goldman Field, which opened in 1932, is home to the California track & field and soccer teams.
Long considered one of the finest track & field facilities in the world, Edwards Stadium has a legacy unmatched in collegiate track & field. Not only has the facility been host to some of the best individual performances in the sport's history, but Edwards Stadium also stands in one of the most beautiful settings in the nation - with panoramic views of the Berkeley Hills and Strawberry Canyon to the east, and San Francisco Bay, the Golden Gate Bridge and the San Francisco skyline to the west.
Over the years, Edwards Stadium has witnessed 12 world records, 26 American records and 24 collegiate records. The first world record set in the stadium was also history's first 15-foot pole vault, by Cornelius "Dutch" Warmerdam in 1940. The last world mark to fall in Berkeley was in 1978, as Washington State's Henry Rono clocked 13:06.4 in the 5,000-meter run. On a cinder surface in 1966 - before a Tartan all-weather surface was added in 1977 - a University of Kansas freshman by the name of Jim Ryun clocked a remarkable 3:51.3 mile.
Named after Col. George C. Edwards, the facility opened in 1932 as the only stadium in the world built for track & field use only. Since that time, Edwards Stadium has hosted eight NCAA and Pac-12 championship meets, a National AAU championship, the All-American Invitational in 1966, and 1971 and '78 USA vs. USSR dual-meets. With a seating capacity of 22,000, Edwards Stadium for years had the distinction of being the largest exclusive track & field facility in the United States.

In 1967, the oval itself was dedicated in the name of Walter Christie, Cal's first track & field coach (1900-32), and in the early 1960's, the "Friends of California Track" raised funds to build the Walter Christie Bench, which stands just outside the running track on the west side of the field.
Beginning with the 1999-20000 school year, the Cal men's and women's soccer teams adopted Edwards Stadium's infield - Goldman Field - as their home venue. The complex opened for soccer prior to the 1999 season, after being converted to a regulation 70-by-115-yards natural grass soccer field.
The improvements for Edwards Stadium were spearheaded by a lead gift of $1.5 million from alumni Richard and Rhoda Goldman. In recognition of their tremendous contribution, the field at the stadium was renamed Goldman Field in honor of Richard's father, Richard Samuel Goldman. In addition, former track athlete David Epstein ('61) made a $250,000 challenge match for other Cal track alumni and friends. Other alumni who have stepped forward with significant support include William Monheit ('33), Frederick Binkley ('43) and Thomas Floers ('48). Below are a list of improvements which have been made.
Following the completion of the renovation project, Edwards Stadium was honored with the 1999-2000 Outstanding Facility Design and Construction award by the U.S. Tennis Court and Track & Field Construction Association.
Most recently, the track received a new all-weather surface prior to the 2013 season.

**_Edwards-Maurer Field,_**_home to Tiger field hockey, football, men's and women's lacrosse, and men's and women's soccer._

## About This Facility
Set adjacent to the Health, Wellness & Athletics (HWA) Complex and encircled by **Earl F. Morris Track** on the north end of Wittenberg's picturesque 100-acre campus, Edwards-Maurer Field serves as the competition home of the Tiger field hockey, football, men's and women's lacrosse, and men's and women's soccer teams. Situated within historic Wittenberg Stadium, Edwards-Maurer Field also hosts outdoor club and intramurals events, in addition to a variety of high school and youth activities throughout the year.
In 2005, the field's knitted nylon artificial surface was replaced with Prestige artificial turf, and a new UBU Sports Speed Series S5-M synthetic turf was laid in 2015. The playing surface is designed to handle year-round, multi-sport use and unpredictable Ohio weather, with the 2015 turf installed by Maumee Bay Turf Center.
The turf upgrade to Edwards-Maurer Field in 2005 coincided with the resurfacing of Earl F. Morris Track with a Recotan surface (work performed by DeFargo Sports Surfaces of Round Rock, Texas), the **opening of the Rosencrans Hall of Honor Fitness Center** and the reconstruction of the staircase leading to the main entrance of the stadium. The men's and women's soccer teams began competing at the field after the installation of the turf, having previously played at Bill Edwards Field, near **Betty Doughman Dillahunt Field**.

## About This Facility
Edwards-Maurer Field stands on a site which has served as the home of Tiger football since 1923, field hockey since 1993, lacrosse since 1968 and soccer since 2005. In 1993, the $2.2 million Bill Edwards Drive Project installed Astroturf, lights (for the first time since 1967) and a new track. On Sept. 8, 1993, a ribbon-cutting ceremony preceded the first intercollegiate game on the new surface, which saw field hockey host Earlham and also served as a celebration of the 100th anniversary of women's athletics at Wittenberg. The dedication of Edwards-Maurer Field occured on Oct. 2, 1993, at halftime of the Homecoming football game vs. Case Western Reserve.
The field has played host to countless Ohio Athletic Conference and North Coast Athletic Conference championships, NCAA Division III postseason games, and regular season thrillers over the years. Even on chilly November nights and wet March afternoons, the Tiger faithful pack the stands.
**Accessibility:** Edwards-Maurer Field and Wittenberg Stadium are fully accessible to individuals with disabilities, and the Athletics staff is happy to make accommodations for interested patrons. The stadium features wheelchair seating at the top of the stands, and both the north and south gates are accessible via wheelchair.
* * *

## About This Facility
###  Bill Edwards
Bill Edwards, Wittenberg class of 1931, was introduced as the university's athletic director and head football coach on April 3, 1955. The Wittenberg University Department of Athletics hasn’t been the same since, rising to a level of prominence in small college athletics that is rivaled by few of its peers.
Edwards, who had high school, college and professional coaching experience before taking a pay cut to return to his alma mater, patrolled the sidelines for three national titles in the 1960s while compiling a 98-20-4 record in 14 years as Wittenberg's head football coach (1955-69). He was later inducted into the National College Football Hall of Fame, one of four Wittenberg athletes or coaches to gain such acclaim, and he was a member of the inaugural class of the university's Athletics Hall of Honor in 1985. He passed away in 1987.
Find more information on his legacy at Wittenberg **in this news release**, commemorating the 50th anniversary of his hiring.
* * *

## About This Facility
###  Dave Maurer
Dave Maurer built a tremendous legacy over 40 years as a coach, administrator and professor. Maurer, a 1987 Wittenberg Athletics Hall of Honor inductee, coached track and field, swimming and diving, and golf at various points during his Wittenberg career, in addition to his well-known exploits on the football sidelines. He also served as the university's director of men's athletics and was a professor of health and physical education. Maurer passed away in 2011 at the age of 79.
After more than a decade as an assistant football coach at Wittenberg, Maurer took the reins in 1969. Through 1983, Maurer posted a career record of 129-23-3, good for an astounding .842 winning percentage, best among active coaches at that time, and he earned national coach of the year honors twice. Along the way, Maurer directed three teams to national championships (and was an assistant coach for two other national titlists) and two teams to NCAA Division III Tournament runner-up finishes. The Tigers went undefeated three times and won seven Ohio Athletic Conference championships in his 15 seasons as head coach, and Maurer was later inducted into the National College Football Hall of Fame.
Find more information on his lasting impact at Wittenberg **in this online feature**, celebrating "Dave Maurer Day" at Wittenberg.
* * *

## About This Facility
### History
The original Wittenberg Stadium _**(pictured left: Zimmerman Field circa 1915)**_ was constructed over 1922 and 1923, and dedicated on Saturday, Oct. 20, of that year, prior to a 14-0 loss to visiting Ohio Wesleyan. Capacity crowds of 5,000 in both the permanent west stands and equally large but temporary east stands, where both student sections were seated, plus standing room only crowds of more than 2,000 set the attendance record of over 12,000. The facility was constructed with concrete stands seating 4,980, at a cost of $100,000. At the time, the _Springfield Daily News_ described the stadium as the second largest college football stadium in Ohio, behind only Ohio Stadium in Columbus, which opened the year before in 1922.
Wittenberg Stadium was built on an abandoned gravel pit directly east of Zimmerman Field, which had served as the school's athletic field since 1902. College President Rees Edgar Tulloss selected the site, and Athletics Director and College Football Hall of Famer Ernie Godfrey and his assistants prepared the playing field. Work on the field included digging out 10,000 cubic yards of earth and replacing it with two feet of conditioned gravel topped by soil and sod at an appropriate slope. Original plans called for the completion of a bowl-type stadium seating 30,000 spectators. Work to secure financing and acquire land began in 1919.
Zimmerman Field had been the first permanent enclosed athletic field at the college before it was succeeded by Wittenberg Stadium. A group of local business leaders led by John L. Zimmerman purchased the land in 1902 and donated it to the school in Zimmerman's name. The first game played at the new field was a scoreless tie with Kenyon on November 27, 1902, the last game of the season.

Last year, a possible new tradition seemed to begin, and it continues in 2026 as the USA Curling Arena National Championship goes to newly christened dedicated curling ice. Dallas/Fort Worth Curling Club is set to host their first national championship in their new facility this week, bringing the event to the most dominant region in the history of arena nationals for the first time.
USA Curling’s Arena National Championships have been held since 2013, and never before has the event been held in the Mid-America region. Despite that, the MACA region has won 4 of 11 championships (three of those by 2026 competitor Alyssa Parks) while the region has been on top of the men’s podium an astounding 8 times. Most of those 8 championships were won by members of Dallas/Fort Worth Curling Club.
Finally, after years of hard work and significant investments of time and money, DFW Curling Club achieved the goal of so many arena clubs: to be ineligible to compete at arena nationals. Their long history of strong showings at nationals is coming to an end for the best reason as they open up their new dedicated facility in Irving, Texas.
The overhead view from Dallas/Fort Worth’s new home in Irving, Texas. Photo: Jim Hicks
It hasn’t been without challenges. If you are on social media, you’ve likely seen that the club was broken into shortly after their grand opening bonspiel last month. Among the stolen items were thousands of dollars’ worth of valuable tools owned by members which were being used in their continued construction.
It was a significant setback for the club in their new facility.
If anything, the arrival of 24 teams from across the country into their new home should be a welcome morale boost. The arriving teams will enter the facility and hopefully take a moment to envision dreams of their own hopeful graduation from arena ice to a new place they can call home.
If you want to help support DFW Curling Club following last months’ break-in so they can recoup some of what they lost and continue making progress on their new home, click the link below:
Donate to Dallas/Fort Worth Curling Club
Let’s dig into this year’s event and meet the teams, learn how to watch, and where to follow along!
DFW Curling offers some streaming through their YouTube channel.

Scores, standings, and a detailed draw schedule can be accessed through the USA Curling event page.
Scores and Standings
Both the men’s and women’s events will feature 12 teams. Because DFW Curling is a 5-sheet club, two teams will be on bye for each draw. The draws will alternate between men’s and women’s draws with the first women’s draw starting at 8pm CST on Wednesday, November 11th.
The top three teams from each pool qualify for the playoffs with the top seed earning a bye into the semifinal.
Teams are listed in order of peer seeding.
Thank you to Austin Binish at 5ucurler.com for helping me compile efficiency statistics referenced below.
Team Asis is back, back again. After qualifying at the Coulee Sweep Last Chance qualifier in La Crosse, Wisconsin a few months ago, Jennifer Asis returns for her fourth consecutive national championship. Teammates Jaclyn Pytlarz and Melissa Wheeler are back for their fifth consecutive event, having played in every championship since it restarted in 2022.
Asis has won a medal of every color over the past three years and is coming off of a bronze medal finish in 2025. The Silicon Valley rink heads back to nationals as an incredibly well-rounded team who posted the best Steal Defense Efficiency rating (not giving up steals when you have hammer) at this championship for the second consecutive year. If they can continue that trend and force their opponents to single points at a high rate, they’ll be in contention for a podium once again.
_Team Asis after their 2024 National Chamiponship in Wausau, WI. Photo: USA Curling_
Jordan Connelly returns for her second consecutive arena national championship after winning the MoPac playdown in back-to-back seasons. Their best-of-three playdown against fellow club members from Team Bonache went the distance, but they emerged victorious. At least year’s championships, Connelly went 3-2 in round robin play before being eliminated in the quarterfinals.

Team Mercer of the Cleveland Skating Club qualified for the Arena National Championship through an uncontested playdown, but don’t let that fool you. This team is in the running every single year at arena nationals. Katy Mercer’s rink has posted fourth-place finishes each of the past two seasons, but they’re no strangers to the podium either. They won gold in 2018 and silver in 2019. They’ll be a tough matchup for everyone and should be considered a playoff contender.
It looked like Kelsey Beyer was on the verge of making the playoffs at last year’s national championship in Las Vegas. The Minnesota rink started the event by beating the eventual national championships, lost a tight game to Jennifer Asis, and entered their final game of pool play with a 2-2 record, just needing a win to qualify. Unfortunately, that last game didn’t go their way.
They boasted the best hammer efficiency rate in the field last year, scoring two points with the hammer in nearly 50% of all of their ends. If they can continue that trend again this season, they’ll have a great chance to advance to the playoffs.
Team Roozee is one of the only newcomers to this year’s championship, qualifying out of the Pacific Northwest region. After falling short against Boise’s Rhiannon Avery last season, it was Roozee who was victorious in the playdown in 2026, sweeping a best-of-three set against last year’s PNWCA representatives and playoff qualifiers. Roozee’s success at playdowns was thanks in large part to their ability to steal at crucial points in both games. It’s a feat that can be difficult to repeat but also can be very frustrating to play against when successful.
The three-year-old Rhinelander Curling Club is sending a team to nationals for the second consecutive year after Team Rice went unopposed in their regional playdown. Though they went winless last year, they lost by just one or two points in three of the games, jumping out to early leads in each. Jean Rice showed her teams can start fast, but the key now becomes finishing strong to earn the team (and club’s) first wins at a national championship. She has a new set of teammates with her this year, and the team has been working hard to improve, traveling to dedicated curling clubs in Wisconsin to get practice ice in preparation for the event.

Team Segovia after winning the MACA Playdowns. Photo: Curling Club of Houston
Multi-time champions Team Segovia is back at arena nationals after a one-year hiatus. The team had to decline their invitation to compete last season, ending the streak of medals for the Curling Club of Houston at the event. Alyssa Parks was on the team for the three consecutive gold medals (2019, 2022, 2023) while Julie Segovia and lead Jessica Bostwick were each there in 2022-2023. Their streak was ended with a silver medal in 2024, but I expect this team to be right back on the podium this season.
Meghan Taylor joins the team at the second position this season, and she has been playing on the women’s tour with Segovia and Parks across the United States and Canada this season. The team qualified for the playoffs at the MCT Atkins Curling Supplies Classic last weekend which should have helped serve as an excellent tune-up for the team.
When Segovia had to step back from last year’s championship, it opened the door for Morgan Andenas-Weber’s team from Sioux Falls to get into the championship. They snuck into the playoffs with a 3-2 record before rattling off three consecutive wins in the playoffs to win their first Arena National Championship.
As the returning champions, they received an automatic invite to this year’s championship, their fourth consecutive appearance. All four members return from last year’s team, and they proved then that all you need is a chance. Can they do it again in 2027?
It’s a new-look team for Rocket City Curling Club this year in what should be their final year of the Arena National Championships. The club’s 5-sheet dedicated curling facility is under construction in Huntsville, Alabama and slated to open early next year.
This may be a new crew to arena nationals, but they’re not lacking in overall experience. The skip Molly Hackett threw fourth rocks at last year’s 5-and-Under National Championship and also plays occasionally on the mixed doubles tour, so I expect them to be well-prepared and a tough opponent. I expect Pool B to give us some fun games and would not be shocked if Hackett snags a playoff spot.

The **Texas Longhorns** are the athletic teams representing the University of Texas at Austin, a public university in Austin, Texas, United States, and the flagship institution of the University of Texas System.

The teams take their name from Longhorn cattle that were an important part of the development of Texas, and are now the official "large animal" of the state of Texas.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-2) The _Longhorn_ nickname had begun appearing in Texas newspapers by 1900,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-3) and is often shortened to the _Horns._ Generally, both the men's and women's teams are referred to as the Longhorns. The mascot is a Texas Longhorn steer named Bevo. The Longhorns have consistently been ranked as the biggest brand in collegiate athletics, in both department size and breadth of appeal.
The University of Texas at Austin offers a wide variety of varsity and intramural sports programs, and was selected as "America's Best Sports College" in a 2002 analysis by _Sports Illustrated_. Texas was also listed as the number one Collegiate Licensing Company client from 2005 to 2013 in regards to the amount of annual trademark royalties received from the sales of its fan merchandise.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-CLC_2013-4)
Until Athletic Director Chris Del Conte altered the organizational structure of the athletic department in 2017,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-5) Texas was the only remaining NCAA Division I school to operate separate men's and women's athletic departments, after the other remaining holdout, the University of Tennessee,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-6) merged its men's and women's athletic departments at the end of the 2011–12 academic year.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-7)

A charter member of the Southwest Conference until its dissolution in 1996, the Texas Longhorns competed in the Big 12 Conference until 2024. The Texas Longhorns joined the Southeastern Conference for the 2024–2025 season with the University of Oklahoma for a reported $100 million,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-8) as a member of the National Collegiate Athletic Association. The school's colors are officially Orange (Pantone 159) and White, with Burnt Orange — also known as Texas Orange – being the specific shade of orange used.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-10)The University of Texas Longhorn Band performs the alma mater as well as the university fight song ("Texas Fight") at various sporting events.
Over the years, Longhorn sports teams have won 56 total national championships,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-11) 47 of which are NCAA National Championships.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-12) The University of Texas currently fields a varsity team in nine men's sports and 12 women's sports.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-13)

In 1992, seven women athletes representing club-level rowing, soccer and gymnastics and intramural softball, organized by the rowing club coach, sued the university in U.S. District Court charging them with Title IX violations. At the time there were more men on the football team than there were varsity-level women athletes. In July 1993 Texas settled the lawsuit, agreeing to add women's rowing, soccer and softball; and agreeing to devote more than 44 percent of its varsity athletic roster spots and more than 42 percent of its athletic scholarship money to women. Women's soccer was added in 1993, softball in 1995 and rowing in 1997.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-14)
Darrell K Royal–Texas Memorial Stadium with a view of the Godzillatron
Two Texas Longhorn running backs have won college football's most prestigious individual award, the Heisman Trophy: Earl Campbell (1977) and Ricky Williams (1998). Seventeen Longhorn players and two Longhorn coaches have been inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-15) while four are enshrined in the Pro Football Hall of Fame.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-16)Other Longhorn players have also received recognition for their performance.

In terms of total wins, Texas is the 2nd-ranked NCAA Division I FBS program in college football history with 891 wins, after passing Nebraska during the 2016 season. As of the end of the 2016 season, the Longhorns' [all-time record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_football's_ten_most_victorious_programs "College football's ten most victorious programs") is 891–359–33 (.709). Only the University of Michigan has won more games and a greater percentage of games played than Texas,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-17) which recorded its 800th victory with the Longhorns' 41–38 win over the USC Trojans in the 2006 BCS National Championship Game at the Rose Bowl. During the late 1980s and early 1990s, the program was somewhat less successful, but the Longhorns have since returned to prominence in college football, finishing in the top six of the AP and coaches' polls in 2001, 2002, 2004, 2005, 2008 and 2009.

The University of Texas team plays home games in Darrell K Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium which has a seating capacity of 100,119.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-DKR_attendance-18) Renovations began on the stadium November 14, 2005, two days following the last home football game of the 2005 season. The improvements were completed before the 2008 football season, and included additional seating[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-19) and the nation's first high definition video display in a collegiate facility nicknamed "Godzillatron".[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-20) The university completed a $27 million expansion and renovation to the south end zone facilities in August 2009 which added 4,525 permanent bleacher seats and changed the playing surface to FieldTurf. With the new permanent bleacher seating section added behind the south end zone and the total remodeling of the north end zone completed in 2008, the stadium's official capacity now stands at 100,119. This was surpassed when 101,357[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-DKR_Facts-21) saw #3-ranked Texas beat Kansas 51–20[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-All-Time_Results-22) on November 21, 2009.

The University of Texas began varsity intercollegiate competition in men's basketball in 1906.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-Timeline-23) The Longhorns rank 18th in total victories among all NCAA Division Icollege basketball programs and 25th in all-time win percentage among programs with at least 60 years in Division I, with an all-time win–loss record of 1791–1088 (.622).[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-NCAA_Record_Book_71-24) Among Big 12 Conference men's basketball programs, Texas is second only to [Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_Jayhawks_men's_basketball "Kansas Jayhawks men's basketball") in both all-time wins and all-time win percentage.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-NCAA_Record_Book_71-24)

Since 1924, the Longhorns have played their home games at Darrell K Royal–Texas Memorial Stadium in Austin, Texas, the ninth largest stadium in the world. The team is represented by their live mascot, Bevo, a Texas Longhorn steer with burnt orange and white coloring. Win or lose, Longhorns fans and players sing 'The Eyes of Texas' before and after every game, alongside their fight song, 'Texas Fight'.
Photograph of the 1893 football team
Beginning in 1893, the Texas Longhorns football program is one of the most highly regarded and historic programs of all time.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-7) From 1936 to 1946 the team was led by Hall of Fame coach Dana X. Bible,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-8) and then from 1957 to 1976 the team was led by Hall of Fame coach Darrell K Royal,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-T-rings-9) who won three national championships.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-10) The first championship was in 1963 (11–0 record, culminating with a Cotton Bowl victory over No. 2 Navy) and the second in 1969 (11–0 record, including a victory over No. 2 Arkansas in the "Game of the Century" and a Cotton Bowl victory over Notre Dame).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-T-rings-9) From 1998 to 2013, the Longhorns were coached by Mack Brown. During Brown's tenure, Texas won two Big 12 Conference championships, and a national championship in 2005 (13–0 record, including a victory over USC in the Rose Bowl). Texas last appeared in a national championship game in 2009, losing to Alabama.

In 2009, ESPN ranked Texas as the seventh-most prestigious college football program since 1936.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-11) In 2012, the football program was valued at $805 million,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-12) more than the calculated value of several NFL teams._[citation needed_] Texas is known for their post-season appearances, ranking second in number of bowl game appearances (55),[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-13) fourth in bowl game victories (29), most Southwest Conference football championships (27), and most Cotton Bowl Classic appearances[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-14) and victories. Other NCAA records include 108 winning seasons out of 122 total seasons, 24 seasons with 10 or more wins, 9 undefeated seasons, and 26 seasons with at most one loss or tie. From 1936 to 2012, the Longhorns football teams have been in the AP or coaches' rankings 66 out of 76 seasons (86.8% of the time), finishing those seasons ranked in the top twenty-five 48 times and the top ten 28 times. Texas claims four Division I-A national championships (1963, 1969, 1970 and 2005) and 33 conference championships (4 Big 12 Conference, 27 Southwest Conference, and 2 Texas Intercollegiate Athletic Association).

A total of 129 (53 consensus and 22 unanimous) Texas players have been named to College Football All-America Teams, while two Longhorn players, Earl Campbell (1977) and Ricky Williams (1998), have won the Heisman Trophy,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-15) "College football's most prestigious individual honor".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-16) Seventeen Longhorns have been inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame, while four are enshrined in the Pro Football Hall of Fame.
At the start of the 2019 season, Texas' all-time record was 909–371–33 (.705), which ranked as the third-most wins.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-18) By the end of the season, Texas' record was 916–375–33 (.704), losing a spot and dropping to fourth in NCAA Division I FBS overall history.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-19)
In July 2021, after 25 seasons as members of the Big 12, Texas and rival Oklahoma accepted invitations to join the Southeastern Conference (SEC) no later than the 2025 season.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-20) In February 2023, the Big 12 announced that the two schools had negotiated a combined $100 million early termination fee in order to leave for the SEC a year before the schools' media rights deal with the Big 12 was set to expire.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-Dinich-21) The Longhorns football team continued competing in the Big 12 through the 2023 season before moving to the SEC in 2024.

Texas joined the Southeastern Conference in 2024.
Texas has been affiliated with four conferences and twice been an independent.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-All-Time_Results-22)
*   Independent (1893–1895, 1905–1912)  
*   Southern Intercollegiate Athletic Association (1896–1904)  
*   Texas Intercollegiate Athletic Association (1909–1914)  
*   Southwest Conference (1915–1995)  
*   Big 12 Conference (1996–2023)  
*   Southeastern Conference (2024–present)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-Dinich-21)
Texas has been selected national champion in 9 seasons from NCAA-designated major selectors, including 4 from the major wire-service: AP Poll and/or Coaches' Poll.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-2017ncaabook-23):107–109 The 1963, 1969, 1970, and 2005 championships are claimed by the school, while the remainder are not claimed.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-24)

The school's colors are officially Orange (Pantone 159) and White, with Burnt Orange — also known as Texas Orange – being the specific shade of orange used.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-10)The University of Texas Longhorn Band performs the alma mater as well as the university fight song ("Texas Fight") at various sporting events.
Over the years, Longhorn sports teams have won 56 total national championships,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-11) 47 of which are NCAA National Championships.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-12) The University of Texas currently fields a varsity team in nine men's sports and 12 women's sports.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-13)
texts.4:
In 1992, seven women athletes representing club-level rowing, soccer and gymnastics and intramural softball, organized by the rowing club coach, sued the university in U.S. District Court charging them with Title IX violations. At the time there were more men on the football team than there were varsity-level women athletes. In July 1993 Texas settled the lawsuit, agreeing to add women's rowing, soccer and softball; and agreeing to devote more than 44 percent of its varsity athletic roster spots and more than 42 percent of its athletic scholarship money to women. Women's soccer was added in 1993, softball in 1995 and rowing in 1997.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-14)
Darrell K Royal–Texas Memorial Stadium with a view of the Godzillatron
Two Texas Longhorn running backs have won college football's most prestigious individual award, the Heisman Trophy: Earl Campbell (1977) and Ricky Williams (1998). Seventeen Longhorn players and two Longhorn coaches have been inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-15) while four are enshrined in the Pro Football Hall of Fame.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-16)Other Longhorn players have also received recognition for their performance.
texts.5: In terms of total wins, Texas is the 2nd-ranked NCAA Division I FBS program in college football history with 891 wins, after passing Nebraska during the 2016 season. As of the end of the 2016 season, the Longhorns' [all-time record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_football's_ten_most_victorious_programs "College football's ten most victorious programs") is 891–359–33 (.709). Only the University of Michigan has won more games and a greater percentage of games played than Texas,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-17) which recorded its 800th victory with the Longhorns' 41–38 win over the USC Trojans in the 2006 BCS National Championship Game at the Rose Bowl. During the late 1980s and early 1990s, the program was somewhat less successful, but the Longhorns have since returned to prominence in college football, finishing in the top six of the AP and coaches' polls in 2001, 2002, 2004, 2005, 2008 and 2009.
texts.6: The University of Texas team plays home games in Darrell K Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium which has a seating capacity of 100,119.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-DKR_attendance-18) Renovations began on the stadium November 14, 2005, two days following the last home football game of the 2005 season. The improvements were completed before the 2008 football season, and included additional seating[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-19) and the nation's first high definition video display in a collegiate facility nicknamed "Godzillatron".[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-20) The university completed a $27 million expansion and renovation to the south end zone facilities in August 2009 which added 4,525 permanent bleacher seats and changed the playing surface to FieldTurf. With the new permanent bleacher seating section added behind the south end zone and the total remodeling of the north end zone completed in 2008, the stadium's official capacity now stands at 100,119. This was surpassed when 101,357[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-DKR_Facts-21) saw #3-ranked Texas beat Kansas 51–20[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-All-Time_Results-22) on November 21, 2009.

Since 1924, the Longhorns have played their home games at Darrell K Royal–Texas Memorial Stadium in Austin, Texas, the ninth largest stadium in the world. The team is represented by their live mascot, Bevo, a Texas Longhorn steer with burnt orange and white coloring. Win or lose, Longhorns fans and players sing 'The Eyes of Texas' before and after every game, alongside their fight song, 'Texas Fight'.
Photograph of the 1893 football team
Beginning in 1893, the Texas Longhorns football program is one of the most highly regarded and historic programs of all time.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-7) From 1936 to 1946 the team was led by Hall of Fame coach Dana X. Bible,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-8) and then from 1957 to 1976 the team was led by Hall of Fame coach Darrell K Royal,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-T-rings-9) who won three national championships.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-10) The first championship was in 1963 (11–0 record, culminating with a Cotton Bowl victory over No. 2 Navy) and the second in 1969 (11–0 record, including a victory over No. 2 Arkansas in the "Game of the Century" and a Cotton Bowl victory over Notre Dame).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-T-rings-9) From 1998 to 2013, the Longhorns were coached by Mack Brown. During Brown's tenure, Texas won two Big 12 Conference championships, and a national championship in 2005 (13–0 record, including a victory over USC in the Rose Bowl). Texas last appeared in a national championship game in 2009, losing to Alabama.
texts.4: In 2009, ESPN ranked Texas as the seventh-most prestigious college football program since 1936.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-11) In 2012, the football program was valued at $805 million,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-12) more than the calculated value of several NFL teams._[citation needed_] Texas is known for their post-season appearances, ranking second in number of bowl game appearances (55),[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-13) fourth in bowl game victories (29), most Southwest Conference football championships (27), and most Cotton Bowl Classic appearances[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-14) and victories. Other NCAA records include 108 winning seasons out of 122 total seasons, 24 seasons with 10 or more wins, 9 undefeated seasons, and 26 seasons with at most one loss or tie. From 1936 to 2012, the Longhorns football teams have been in the AP or coaches' rankings 66 out of 76 seasons (86.8% of the time), finishing those seasons ranked in the top twenty-five 48 times and the top ten 28 times. Texas claims four Division I-A national championships (1963, 1969, 1970 and 2005) and 33 conference championships (4 Big 12 Conference, 27 Southwest Conference, and 2 Texas Intercollegiate Athletic Association).
texts.5:
A total of 129 (53 consensus and 22 unanimous) Texas players have been named to College Football All-America Teams, while two Longhorn players, Earl Campbell (1977) and Ricky Williams (1998), have won the Heisman Trophy,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-15) "College football's most prestigious individual honor".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-16) Seventeen Longhorns have been inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame, while four are enshrined in the Pro Football Hall of Fame.
At the start of the 2019 season, Texas' all-time record was 909–371–33 (.705), which ranked as the third-most wins.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-18) By the end of the season, Texas' record was 916–375–33 (.704), losing a spot and dropping to fourth in NCAA Division I FBS overall history.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-19)
In July 2021, after 25 seasons as members of the Big 12, Texas and rival Oklahoma accepted invitations to join the Southeastern Conference (SEC) no later than the 2025 season.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-20) In February 2023, the Big 12 announced that the two schools had negotiated a combined $100 million early termination fee in order to leave for the SEC a year before the schools' media rights deal with the Big 12 was set to expire.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-Dinich-21) The Longhorns football team continued competing in the Big 12 through the 2023 season before moving to the SEC in 2024.

The **Texas Longhorns** are the athletic teams representing the University of Texas at Austin, a public university in Austin, Texas, United States, and the flagship institution of the University of Texas System.

The teams take their name from Longhorn cattle that were an important part of the development of Texas, and are now the official "large animal" of the state of Texas.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-2) The _Longhorn_ nickname had begun appearing in Texas newspapers by 1900,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-3) and is often shortened to the _Horns._ Generally, both the men's and women's teams are referred to as the Longhorns. The mascot is a Texas Longhorn steer named Bevo. The Longhorns have consistently been ranked as the biggest brand in collegiate athletics, in both department size and breadth of appeal.
The University of Texas at Austin offers a wide variety of varsity and intramural sports programs, and was selected as "America's Best Sports College" in a 2002 analysis by _Sports Illustrated_. Texas was also listed as the number one Collegiate Licensing Company client from 2005 to 2013 in regards to the amount of annual trademark royalties received from the sales of its fan merchandise.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-CLC_2013-4)

During the late 1980s and early 1990s, the program was somewhat less successful, but the Longhorns have since returned to prominence in college football, finishing in the top six of the AP and coaches' polls in 2001, 2002, 2004, 2005, 2008 and 2009.

The University of Texas team plays home games in Darrell K Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium which has a seating capacity of 100,119.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-DKR_attendance-18) Renovations began on the stadium November 14, 2005, two days following the last home football game of the 2005 season. The improvements were completed before the 2008 football season, and included additional seating[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-19) and the nation's first high definition video display in a collegiate facility nicknamed "Godzillatron".[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-20) The university completed a $27 million expansion and renovation to the south end zone facilities in August 2009 which added 4,525 permanent bleacher seats and changed the playing surface to FieldTurf. With the new permanent bleacher seating section added behind the south end zone and the total remodeling of the north end zone completed in 2008, the stadium's official capacity now stands at 100,119. This was surpassed when 101,357[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-DKR_Facts-21) saw #3-ranked Texas beat Kansas 51–20[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-All-Time_Results-22) on November 21, 2009.

Since 1924, the Longhorns have played their home games at Darrell K Royal–Texas Memorial Stadium in Austin, Texas, the ninth largest stadium in the world. The team is represented by their live mascot, Bevo, a Texas Longhorn steer with burnt orange and white coloring. Win or lose, Longhorns fans and players sing 'The Eyes of Texas' before and after every game, alongside their fight song, 'Texas Fight'.
Photograph of the 1893 football team
Beginning in 1893, the Texas Longhorns football program is one of the most highly regarded and historic programs of all time.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-7) From 1936 to 1946 the team was led by Hall of Fame coach Dana X. Bible,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-8) and then from 1957 to 1976 the team was led by Hall of Fame coach Darrell K Royal,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-T-rings-9) who won three national championships.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-10) The first championship was in 1963 (11–0 record, culminating with a Cotton Bowl victory over No. 2 Navy) and the second in 1969 (11–0 record, including a victory over No. 2 Arkansas in the "Game of the Century" and a Cotton Bowl victory over Notre Dame).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-T-rings-9) From 1998 to 2013, the Longhorns were coached by Mack Brown. During Brown's tenure, Texas won two Big 12 Conference championships, and a national championship in 2005 (13–0 record, including a victory over USC in the Rose Bowl). Texas last appeared in a national championship game in 2009, losing to Alabama.

In 2009, ESPN ranked Texas as the seventh-most prestigious college football program since 1936.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-11) In 2012, the football program was valued at $805 million,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-12) more than the calculated value of several NFL teams._[citation needed_] Texas is known for their post-season appearances, ranking second in number of bowl game appearances (55),[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-13) fourth in bowl game victories (29), most Southwest Conference football championships (27), and most Cotton Bowl Classic appearances[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-14) and victories. Other NCAA records include 108 winning seasons out of 122 total seasons, 24 seasons with 10 or more wins, 9 undefeated seasons, and 26 seasons with at most one loss or tie. From 1936 to 2012, the Longhorns football teams have been in the AP or coaches' rankings 66 out of 76 seasons (86.8% of the time), finishing those seasons ranked in the top twenty-five 48 times and the top ten 28 times. Texas claims four Division I-A national championships (1963, 1969, 1970 and 2005) and 33 conference championships (4 Big 12 Conference, 27 Southwest Conference, and 2 Texas Intercollegiate Athletic Association).

A total of 129 (53 consensus and 22 unanimous) Texas players have been named to College Football All-America Teams, while two Longhorn players, Earl Campbell (1977) and Ricky Williams (1998), have won the Heisman Trophy,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-15) "College football's most prestigious individual honor".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-16) Seventeen Longhorns have been inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame, while four are enshrined in the Pro Football Hall of Fame.
At the start of the 2019 season, Texas' all-time record was 909–371–33 (.705), which ranked as the third-most wins.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-18) By the end of the season, Texas' record was 916–375–33 (.704), losing a spot and dropping to fourth in NCAA Division I FBS overall history.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-19)
In July 2021, after 25 seasons as members of the Big 12, Texas and rival Oklahoma accepted invitations to join the Southeastern Conference (SEC) no later than the 2025 season.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-20) In February 2023, the Big 12 announced that the two schools had negotiated a combined $100 million early termination fee in order to leave for the SEC a year before the schools' media rights deal with the Big 12 was set to expire.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-Dinich-21) The Longhorns football team continued competing in the Big 12 through the 2023 season before moving to the SEC in 2024.

Texas joined the Southeastern Conference in 2024.
Texas has been affiliated with four conferences and twice been an independent.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-All-Time_Results-22)
*   Independent (1893–1895, 1905–1912)  
*   Southern Intercollegiate Athletic Association (1896–1904)  
*   Texas Intercollegiate Athletic Association (1909–1914)  
*   Southwest Conference (1915–1995)  
*   Big 12 Conference (1996–2023)  
*   Southeastern Conference (2024–present)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-Dinich-21)
Texas has been selected national champion in 9 seasons from NCAA-designated major selectors, including 4 from the major wire-service: AP Poll and/or Coaches' Poll.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-2017ncaabook-23):107–109 The 1963, 1969, 1970, and 2005 championships are claimed by the school, while the remainder are not claimed.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_football#cite_note-24)

The **Texas Longhorns** are the athletic teams representing the University of Texas at Austin, a public university in Austin, Texas, United States, and the flagship institution of the University of Texas System.

The teams take their name from Longhorn cattle that were an important part of the development of Texas, and are now the official "large animal" of the state of Texas.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-2) The _Longhorn_ nickname had begun appearing in Texas newspapers by 1900,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-3) and is often shortened to the _Horns._ Generally, both the men's and women's teams are referred to as the Longhorns. The mascot is a Texas Longhorn steer named Bevo. The Longhorns have consistently been ranked as the biggest brand in collegiate athletics, in both department size and breadth of appeal.
The University of Texas at Austin offers a wide variety of varsity and intramural sports programs, and was selected as "America's Best Sports College" in a 2002 analysis by _Sports Illustrated_. Texas was also listed as the number one Collegiate Licensing Company client from 2005 to 2013 in regards to the amount of annual trademark royalties received from the sales of its fan merchandise.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-CLC_2013-4)
Until Athletic Director Chris Del Conte altered the organizational structure of the athletic department in 2017,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-5) Texas was the only remaining NCAA Division I school to operate separate men's and women's athletic departments, after the other remaining holdout, the University of Tennessee,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-6) merged its men's and women's athletic departments at the end of the 2011–12 academic year.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-7)

A charter member of the Southwest Conference until its dissolution in 1996, the Texas Longhorns competed in the Big 12 Conference until 2024. The Texas Longhorns joined the Southeastern Conference for the 2024–2025 season with the University of Oklahoma for a reported $100 million,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-8) as a member of the National Collegiate Athletic Association. The school's colors are officially Orange (Pantone 159) and White, with Burnt Orange — also known as Texas Orange – being the specific shade of orange used.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-10)The University of Texas Longhorn Band performs the alma mater as well as the university fight song ("Texas Fight") at various sporting events.
Over the years, Longhorn sports teams have won 56 total national championships,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-11) 47 of which are NCAA National Championships.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-12) The University of Texas currently fields a varsity team in nine men's sports and 12 women's sports.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-13)

In 1992, seven women athletes representing club-level rowing, soccer and gymnastics and intramural softball, organized by the rowing club coach, sued the university in U.S. District Court charging them with Title IX violations. At the time there were more men on the football team than there were varsity-level women athletes. In July 1993 Texas settled the lawsuit, agreeing to add women's rowing, soccer and softball; and agreeing to devote more than 44 percent of its varsity athletic roster spots and more than 42 percent of its athletic scholarship money to women. Women's soccer was added in 1993, softball in 1995 and rowing in 1997.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-14)
Darrell K Royal–Texas Memorial Stadium with a view of the Godzillatron
Two Texas Longhorn running backs have won college football's most prestigious individual award, the Heisman Trophy: Earl Campbell (1977) and Ricky Williams (1998). Seventeen Longhorn players and two Longhorn coaches have been inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-15) while four are enshrined in the Pro Football Hall of Fame.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-16)Other Longhorn players have also received recognition for their performance.

The **Texas Longhorns** are the athletic teams representing the University of Texas at Austin, a public university in Austin, Texas, United States, and the flagship institution of the University of Texas System.
texts.1:
The teams take their name from Longhorn cattle that were an important part of the development of Texas, and are now the official "large animal" of the state of Texas.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-2) The _Longhorn_ nickname had begun appearing in Texas newspapers by 1900,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-3) and is often shortened to the _Horns._ Generally, both the men's and women's teams are referred to as the Longhorns. The mascot is a Texas Longhorn steer named Bevo. The Longhorns have consistently been ranked as the biggest brand in collegiate athletics, in both department size and breadth of appeal.
The University of Texas at Austin offers a wide variety of varsity and intramural sports programs, and was selected as "America's Best Sports College" in a 2002 analysis by _Sports Illustrated_. Texas was also listed as the number one Collegiate Licensing Company client from 2005 to 2013 in regards to the amount of annual trademark royalties received from the sales of its fan merchandise.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-CLC_2013-4)
Until Athletic Director Chris Del Conte altered the organizational structure of the athletic department in 2017,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-5) Texas was the only remaining NCAA Division I school to operate separate men's and women's athletic departments, after the other remaining holdout, the University of Tennessee,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-6) merged its men's and women's athletic departments at the end of the 2011–12 academic year.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-7)

texts.3:
A charter member of the Southwest Conference until its dissolution in 1996, the Texas Longhorns competed in the Big 12 Conference until 2024. The Texas Longhorns joined the Southeastern Conference for the 2024–2025 season with the University of Oklahoma for a reported $100 million,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-8) as a member of the National Collegiate Athletic Association. The school's colors are officially Orange (Pantone 159) and White, with Burnt Orange — also known as Texas Orange – being the specific shade of orange used.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-10)The University of Texas Longhorn Band performs the alma mater as well as the university fight song ("Texas Fight") at various sporting events.
Over the years, Longhorn sports teams have won 56 total national championships,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-11) 47 of which are NCAA National Championships.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-12) The University of Texas currently fields a varsity team in nine men's sports and 12 women's sports.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-13)
texts.4:
In 1992, seven women athletes representing club-level rowing, soccer and gymnastics and intramural softball, organized by the rowing club coach, sued the university in U.S. District Court charging them with Title IX violations. At the time there were more men on the football team than there were varsity-level women athletes. In July 1993 Texas settled the lawsuit, agreeing to add women's rowing, soccer and softball; and agreeing to devote more than 44 percent of its varsity athletic roster spots and more than 42 percent of its athletic scholarship money to women. Women's soccer was added in 1993, softball in 1995 and rowing in 1997.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-14)
Darrell K Royal–Texas Memorial Stadium with a view of the Godzillatron
Two Texas Longhorn running backs have won college football's most prestigious individual award, the Heisman Trophy: Earl Campbell (1977) and Ricky Williams (1998). Seventeen Longhorn players and two Longhorn coaches have been inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-15) while four are enshrined in the Pro Football Hall of Fame.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-16)Other Longhorn players have also received recognition for their performance.

The **Texas Longhorns** are the athletic teams representing the University of Texas at Austin, a public university in Austin, Texas, United States, and the flagship institution of the University of Texas System.

The teams take their name from Longhorn cattle that were an important part of the development of Texas, and are now the official "large animal" of the state of Texas.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-2) The _Longhorn_ nickname had begun appearing in Texas newspapers by 1900,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-3) and is often shortened to the _Horns._ Generally, both the men's and women's teams are referred to as the Longhorns. The mascot is a Texas Longhorn steer named Bevo. The Longhorns have consistently been ranked as the biggest brand in collegiate athletics, in both department size and breadth of appeal.
The University of Texas at Austin offers a wide variety of varsity and intramural sports programs, and was selected as "America's Best Sports College" in a 2002 analysis by _Sports Illustrated_. Texas was also listed as the number one Collegiate Licensing Company client from 2005 to 2013 in regards to the amount of annual trademark royalties received from the sales of its fan merchandise.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-CLC_2013-4)
Until Athletic Director Chris Del Conte altered the organizational structure of the athletic department in 2017,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-5) Texas was the only remaining NCAA Division I school to operate separate men's and women's athletic departments, after the other remaining holdout, the University of Tennessee,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-6) merged its men's and women's athletic departments at the end of the 2011–12 academic year.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-7)

A charter member of the Southwest Conference until its dissolution in 1996, the Texas Longhorns competed in the Big 12 Conference until 2024. The Texas Longhorns joined the Southeastern Conference for the 2024–2025 season with the University of Oklahoma for a reported $100 million,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-8) as a member of the National Collegiate Athletic Association. The school's colors are officially Orange (Pantone 159) and White, with Burnt Orange — also known as Texas Orange – being the specific shade of orange used.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-10)The University of Texas Longhorn Band performs the alma mater as well as the university fight song ("Texas Fight") at various sporting events.
Over the years, Longhorn sports teams have won 56 total national championships,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-11) 47 of which are NCAA National Championships.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-12) The University of Texas currently fields a varsity team in nine men's sports and 12 women's sports.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-13)

In 1992, seven women athletes representing club-level rowing, soccer and gymnastics and intramural softball, organized by the rowing club coach, sued the university in U.S. District Court charging them with Title IX violations. At the time there were more men on the football team than there were varsity-level women athletes. In July 1993 Texas settled the lawsuit, agreeing to add women's rowing, soccer and softball; and agreeing to devote more than 44 percent of its varsity athletic roster spots and more than 42 percent of its athletic scholarship money to women. Women's soccer was added in 1993, softball in 1995 and rowing in 1997.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-14)
Darrell K Royal–Texas Memorial Stadium with a view of the Godzillatron
Two Texas Longhorn running backs have won college football's most prestigious individual award, the Heisman Trophy: Earl Campbell (1977) and Ricky Williams (1998). Seventeen Longhorn players and two Longhorn coaches have been inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-15) while four are enshrined in the Pro Football Hall of Fame.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns#cite_note-16)Other Longhorn players have also received recognition for their performance.
